heading.en: Finding a needle in a list

hook.en: Your name is somewhere on a long admission list pinned to the notice board. If the list is not in any order, the only way is to read it from the top, one name at a time. That is *linear search*.

say.en: Your name is somewhere on a long admission list pinned to the notice board. If the list is not in any order, the only way is to read it from the top, one name at a time. That is linear search. In this lesson: Define searching and the key.
Trace linear search on a list.
Count comparisons in the best and worst case.

body.en: Searching means locating a particular element, called the key, in a collection of elements; the search is successful if the key is found and unsuccessful otherwise. Linear (sequential) search compares the key with each element of the list in turn, starting from the first. It stops as soon as a match is found and reports the position; if the end of the list is reached without a match, the key is not present. *Linear search* works on both sorted and unsorted lists.

points.en: Key = the element we look for

body.en: A function linear_search(lst, key) uses a for loop over the indices of the list. If lst[index] == key it returns index + 1, the position; after the loop it returns None to show that the key was not found. For a list of n elements the number of comparisons is 1 in the best case (key first) and n in the worst case (key last or absent).
